newsitem.title: IRAN: FEATURE-On Iranian island, Shah's casino changes with the times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-On Iranian island, Shah's casino changes with the times.

text.p: The late Shah of Iran might not have approved what Tehran's more egalitarian Islamic rulers have done to his exclusive casino on this tiny Gulf coral island.

The crown-shaped luxury casino which was built by Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi had just a couple of year's life before falling into neglect after he was toppled in Iran's turbulent revolution in 1979 and the Iran-Iraq war broke out a year later.

It has been refurbished and converted into a high-tech amusement arcade and family restaurant to attract ordinary Iranian tourists rather than guests of the Shah, some of whom were flown by Concorde planes from Paris.

"Kish today...symbolizes one of the blessings of the Islamic Revolution. It is no longer a private leisure resort for the court members, the former royal family and their guests," Mohammad Reza Yazdan Panah, head of the island's free zone organisation, declares in a vistors' guidebook.
VIRTUAL REALITY ATTRACTS VISITORS

"Game's World" is one of the entertainments the government is using to change the resort from an exclusive, invite-only retreat into a mass tourist centre and a free trade zone with more liberal investment laws than the mainland.
The aim is to offer holidays to those Iranians who cannot go abroad either because of lack of money or difficulties in getting visas from foreign governments.
Kish authorities are also banking on attracting foreign investment with relaxed ownership and taxation rules.
Card decks, roulette wheels, croupiers and complimentary alcoholic drinks are out and replaced at "Game's World" by state-of-the-art Japanese virtual reality games and pinball.
Red carpets, smoke-glass windows and ceiling decorations that would have graced the Shah's casino are still there, if slightly the worse for wear after some 20 years.
Its attractions scream out for visitors to strap themselves into a simulated cockpit of an American F-16 fighter plane or a tank advancing across a Middle East desert landscape.
For others there are two snooker tables or a small pier outside the building for leisurely and more sedate walks on the sea front.

The Shah's plans for a golf course covering a large stretch of the 90 sq km (35 sq mile) island have been superseded by easy shopping, single-sex beaches, cycle routes, a small zoo and recreational activities such as boating and camel riding.
SHOP TILL YOU DROP
Brightly lit roadside billboards advertising Philips and Panasonic electronic goods show a healthy re-export trade back to the mainland, just 19 km (12 miles) away.
Kish has 12 bazaars some containing up to 200 shops which sell a host of goods including Mickey Mouse toys, foreign clothing and Reebok and Adidas accessories.
Iranian families can be seen at Kish airport lugging music stereos and perfumes back to the mainland after enjoying a brief vacation on the island.
A DIFFERENT IRAN
Kish, which in one promotional poster from the island's free zone organisation is hailed as "The Land of Tranquillizing", is somewhat different from the rest of Iran.
Satellite television, officially banned on the mainland, beams Cable News Network (CNN) and British Broadcasting Corp's (BBC) news broadcasts into Kish hotel rooms.

Stiff currency regulations are relaxed allowing the local rial to trade at 4,580 to the U.S. dollar compared to the official rate of 3,000 rials -- more in line with rates in Tehran's outlawed currency black market.

Foreigners do not need entry visas though social codes on the island, particularly for women who have to remain covered and are not encouraged to mix with men outside the immediate family, are still observed.
The island is dotted with cranes building small-scale businesses, housing and industrial projects such as a planned foreign-backed car factory.
Three hotels and a number of private villas which were in the final stages of completion before the revolution are being renovated to house tourists and business investors.
